We would like to sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive comments on our work. We take every comment seriously and hope our response can address the reviewer’s concerns. If there are any remaining questions, we are more than happy to address them.

---

**Q1: The related work of subject-driven generation**

A1: We appreciate the reviewer for these highly related papers. We will cite and discuss them in the revision. In fact, some of these papers are parallel contributions compared to ours. For example, DisenBooth uses LoRA to finetune the neural network, and it can naturally be replaced by OFT.

---

**Q2: Difference between COFT and OFT**

A2: The motivation of COFT is to constrain the deviation from the pretrained model in order to improve finetuning stability. In terms of the best possible performance, OFT and COFT may be similar, but COFT generally yields better finetuning stability and is less sensitive to the number of finetuning iterations. Determining a good finetuning iteration is actually highly nontrivial yet important. We have empirically verified that COFT can finetune the model with a very large number of iterations (e.g. 100,000 iterations) while still outputting very plausible results. In contrast, OFT is usually unable to do so. Please refer to Appendix E in our paper for more results.

The constrained version of OFT is in fact another advantage over LoRA, because it is nontrivial in LoRA to add a constraint such that the finetuned weight will not deviate too much from the pretrain weight. In OFT, setting a good $\epsilon$ for the difference between the orthogonal matrix and the identity matrix is simple, while in LoRA, it is nontrivial to set a good $\epsilon$ between the pretrained weight matrix and the finetuned weight matrix.

---

**Q3: no specific-domain finetuning comparisons between OFT and LoRA**

A3: Great suggestion! We follow the reviewer’s suggestion and add a downstream finetuning experiment. For quantitative comparison, we finetune the original Stable Diffusion with the text-to-image diffusion loss on the MS-COCO training set. For evaluation, we use the text prompt from the MS-COCO validation set to generate images, and then compare it to the original MS-COCO validation set to calculate the FID score. The results are summarized in the following table:

|Metric|SD (no finetuning)|SD (full param)|SD (LoRA)|SD (OFT)|
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|**FID**|29.0|25.9|25.0|**24.6**|

From the FID results, we can observe that OFT outperforms both full parameter finetuning and LoRA.

For qualitative comparison,we additionally evaluate our proposed method by finetuning the pre-trained Stable Diffusion model on other datasets, to generate images of different styles. We evaluated two different scenarios, including generating sketches (by finetuning on the **sketch-scene** dataset, which includes 10k caption-sketch pairs) and art images (by finetuning on the **wikiart_captions** datasheet, 81.4k caption-image pairs). For testing, we simply run inference on the finetuned model, using the captions from the MS-COCO validation set. The qualitative results can be found in Figure 2&3 in the **Rebuttal PDF**.

We will add these experiments and results to the revision.

---

**Q4: Orthogonal transformation is a sweet spot between flexibility and regularity. How can you draw the conclusion?**

A4: Sorry for the confusion. Our conclusion that orthogonal transformation is a good tradeoff between flexibility and regularity mostly comes from the empirical evidence in Figure 3 of the main paper, where unconstrained linear transformation completely fails to finetune the model. While identity matrices do not have any flexibility of finetuning the model, we observe that orthogonal matrices have sufficient regularity to achieve flexible yet stable finetuning. Another motivation that drives us to use orthogonal transformation is its perfect preservation of hyperspherical energy, as shown in Figure 1 of the main paper. We will add more discussion and justification in the revision.

---

**Q5: In Figure 3, the results of controlnet without orthogonal finetuning (the original controlnet training?) seem to collapse totally. Is it reasonable?**

A5: Sorry for the confusion. This experiment is not conducted with the ControlNet pipeline (which uses an additional branch to add control signals). Instead, we perform this controllable generation task with the finetuning pipeline (what LoRA and OFT use). This experiment aims to show that, without constraining the transformation matrix $R$ (in Eq.2) to be orthogonal, the multiplicative finetuning will fail completely. In contrast, enforcing $R$ to be orthogonal achieves good finetuning performance. The results show the importance of orthogonality in OFT. We apologize for missing experimental details, and we will provide all the details as well as the source code for reproducing this experiment in the revised paper.

---

**Q6: In line 197, why you define HE(W) as this equation**

A6: Thanks for the comment. We define this energy for the sake of notation simplicity. This definition also follows from the paper [Learning towards minimum hyperspherical energy, NeurIPS 2018].

---

**Q7: In line 218, how to ensure that Q is a skew-symmetric matrix in implementation?**

A7: Thanks for the comment. Since the skew-symmetric matrix $A$ is defined to satisfy $A^\top=-A$, where the diagonal is zero. Therefore, we only need to initialize the upper triangular part of $A$ and make them trainable. The lower triangular part of $A$ will simply be copied as the negative version of the upper triangular part. Our source code will be made publicly available. 

---

**Q8: no conclusion & limitation section.**

A8: We are very sorry for not including a conclusion section due to the page limit. We will add a conclusion and limitation section in the revision. For the intended conclusion section, please refer to Q1 of Reviewer styH.

**Q1: DB does not add additional inference overhead (L. 293)**

A1: Good catch and sorry for the mistake. DreamBooth indeed does not introduce inference overhead, but it finetunes much more parameters than OFT. We will correct this mistake in the revision.

---

**Q2: Although the idea makes sense, and is an interesting way to see the problem, it is hard to know whether the empirical improvements are enough. Specifically, it seems like some metrics are better (subject fidelity, quality) and some are worse (prompt fidelity, by very little, could be negligible). But there is no user study, which could put these results in perspective. These metrics are not nearly as strong as a user study and a user study could show the real benefits of the method. This is my main reservation with regards to this work.**

A2: Great suggestion! We follow the reviewer’s suggestion and perform user study to evaluate the generated results in subject-driven generation.

**Human evaluation settings**: we randomly select 7 subjects. For each subject, we randomly select 4 text prompts. Then we have 28 subject-driven generation tasks. For each task, we have one random sample from each method (DreamBooth, LoRA, OFT), and then ask each participant three questions: (1) which image has the subject's identity been preserved the best? I.e., the subject resembles the subject in the sample images; [Subject Fidelity] (2) which image matches the text description the most? [Text Alignment] (3) which image has the best overall quality? [Overall Image Quality]. We have 50 participants in total. We evaluate the methods at two different stages of fine-tuning: at iteration 1000 (where the evaluated methods achieve the overall best performance) and at iteration 10000 (where we evaluate the finetuning stability by continuing the finetuning process). The number below is the percentage of the participants that select the corresponding image.

The results are given as follows:

|| | Iteration 1000| | | Iteration 10000| |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|**Metric**|**DreamBooth**|**LoRA**|**OFT**|**DreamBooth**|**LoRA**|**OFT**|
|**Subject Fidelity**|42.0%|15.4%|**42.6%**|22.4%|1.4%|**76.2%**|
|**Text Alignment**|18.6%|24.7%|**56.7%**|2.6%|1.4%|**96.0%**|
|**Overall Image Quality**|35.7%|19.2%|**45.1%**|11.6%|0.8%|**87.6%**|


We will add all the experimental details and the complete results to the revised paper.

---

**Q3: My second reservation is that, for low ranks, it would be great to have comparisons with LoRA (w/ equal number of parameters, since OFT is more parameter efficient at equal rank)**

A3: Great suggestion! The current experimental setting is to select the best possible hyperparameter (e.g., rank in LoRA, number of blocks in OFT) for all the finetuning methods. For the published methods, we generally start with the official repository and tune the hyperparameter via cross-validation. For example, we find that setting rank as 8 in LoRA yields the best performance, and keeping increasing the rank will actually hurt the performance. Therefore, our OFT already compares with the best setting of LoRA.

In order to fully address the reviewer’s concern, we vary the number of finetuning parameters in LoRA (i.e. varying the rank), and compare their performance to OFT in the segmentation-to-image controllable generation task. The results are as follows 

|Method|LoRA (r=32)|LoRA (r=64)|OFT (block=4)|
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
|**# of params**|13.1 M|23.1 M|16.3 M|
|**mIoU**|23.12|23.05|**27.06**|
|**mAcc**|35.19|35.34|**40.09**|
|**aAcc**|57.64|57.63|**62.42**|

---

**Q4: Societal impact seems to be missing, although is an extension of other personalization methods such as Dreambooth etc. Failure cases would be important for this paper - specifically, when does OFT do less well than LoRA or DB?**

A4: Great suggestion! We have provided some failure cases in Appendix H. In general, we hardly observe cases where DreamBooth can succeed but OFT fails, but as our qualitative results show, there are many cases where DreamBooth fails but OFT works well. The failure cases observed in our experiments usually happen in both DreamBooth and OFT. One common failure case of OFT is the incorrect text grounding in images. For example, we enter a text prompt “a red cat on a black carpet”, OFT will sometimes output images like “a black cat on a red carpet”. However, this also happens in DreamBooth. This is likely due to the grounding problems in CLIP, rather than the problems in finetuning.

Therefore, we definitely agree with the reviewer that failure cases are important, and we will add more failure cases, in-depth discussions and societal impact to the revision.

**Q4: Why finetuning aims to train the model while implicitly minimizing $||M-M^0||$**

A4: The claim comes from a simple derivation. We have one-step gradient descent as $M^1=M^0-\eta\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial M}$, where $\eta$ is the learning rate. Then we have that
$||M^1-M^0||=||M^0-\eta\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial M}-M^0||=\eta||\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial M}||$. Therefore, a smaller learning rate $\eta$ implicitly enforces a smaller difference between $M$ and $M^0$.

OFT does not introduce any computational overhead at inference, making the sampling time at testing exactly the same as the pretrained model (with the same # of steps).

As an example, we compare OFT and LoRA in controllable generation. The runtime comparison is given below:

Therefore, in this simple example, DreamBooth and COFT/OFT perform similarly.  We provide the updated result in the figure 1 of the **Rebuttal PDF**. **Q1: On OFT in section 3.2 and COFT in section 3.4: Can they help learning weight matrices that are identity matrices? From equation (4), it seems COFT can learn this. Did you perform any analysis on the weights to see if the weight matrix can be identity? Would be great if you provide some details in the rebuttal.**

A1: Thanks for the question. If the reviewer is referring to learning a transformation matrix that is an identity matrix, then both OFT and COFT can learn this. In fact, both OFT and COFT initialize the transformation matrix $R$ as an identity matrix such that the finetuning will begin exactly from the pretrained model (similar to the role of zero initialization in existing finetuning methods). The reviewer has the right insight in the sense that, compared to COFT, OFT typically deviates more from the identity matrix due to the lack of identity constraint. After the OFT/COFT finetuning, the transformation matrix $R$ is usually not an identity matrix, otherwise the finetuned model will be exactly the same as the pretrained model. For the weight matrices in the pretrained neural networks, they are usually rectangular matrices and are not identity matrices in practice (especially when they are pretrained).

As an additional benefit of OFT/COFT, we can effortlessly remove the transformation matrix to recover the original pretrained model, while the full parameter finetuning can not easily recover the pretrained model. We also have conducted an empirical analysis to see whether the orthogonality of the transformation matrix is preserved. The reviewer can refer to Figure 1 in the main paper for this result.

If the reviewer still has questions regarding this issue, we are more than happy to provide more details on any follow-up questions.

---

**Q2: In section 5.1, it is not clear if the paper applies OFT and COFT to the CLIP Text encoder as well?**

A2: Thanks for the question. In our experiments, we don’t apply OFT and COFT to the CLIP text encoder. We generally follow the common practice in LoRA which only finetunes the cross-attention layers. Our method finetunes exactly the same layers as LoRA in order to ensure a fair comparison. We will add more related experimental details and also release our source code to ensure full reproducibility.

**Conclusion and future work**: Motivated by the observation that angular information among neurons crucially determines visual semantics, we propose a simple yet effective finetuning method – orthogonal finetuning for controlling text-to-image diffusion models. Specifically, we target two text-to-image applications: subject-driven generation and controllable generation. Compared to existing methods, OFT demonstrates stronger controllability and finetuning stability with fewer number of finetuning parameters. More importantly, OFT does not introduce additional inference overhead, leading to an efficient deployable model.

OFT also introduces a few interesting open problems. First, OFT guarantees the orthogonality via Cayley parametrization which involves a matrix inverse. It slightly limits the scalability of OFT. Although we address this limitation using block diagonal parametrization, how to speed up this matrix inverse in a differentiable way remains a challenge. Second, OFT has unique potential in compositionality, in the sense that the orthogonal matrices produced by multiple OFT finetuning tasks can be multiplied together and remains an orthogonal matrix. Whether this set of orthogonal matrices preserve the knowledge of all the downstream tasks remains an interesting direction to study.

However, the finetuning stability of OFT is much stronger than DreamBooth, since OFT performs significantly better than DreamBooth with a large number of finetuning iterations.

summary.value: The paper introduces a principled finetuning method called Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) for adapting text-to-image diffusion models to different downstream tasks. The key idea of the proposed approach is to preserve hyperspherical energy which characterizes the pairwise neuron relationship on the unit hypersphere. The paper claims that this property is crucial for preserving the semantic generation ability of T2I models. The paper additionally proposes  Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) to improve finetuning stability. Experiments on subject-driven generation and controllable generation demonstrate the utility of the proposed approach.

strengths.value: The key idea of the paper to learn a layer-shared orthogonal transformation for neurons such that their pairwise angles are preserved is interesting and well-presented. The proposed finetuning approach could be potentially useful/applied to other domains/tasks. The experiment results on subject-driven generation and controllable generation are solid with sufficient comparison to the baselines.

weaknesses.value: I do not find any major weaknesses with this work except for few clarification questions: (a) On OFT in section 3.2 and COFT in section 3.4: Can they help learning weight matrices that are identity matrices? From equation (4), it seems COFT can learn this. Did you perform any analysis on the weights to see if the weight matrix can be identity? Would be great if you provide some details in the rebuttal. (b) In section 5.1, it is not clear if the paper applies OFT and COFT to the CLIP Text encoder as well?

summary.value: The paper proposes a method for efficiently fine-tuning pre-trained text-to-image generation models, good results are obtained in experiments.

strengths.value:
The paper proposes OFT and COFT, which can efficiently fine-tune the pre-trained text-to-image generation model as less parameters needed to be fine-tuned compared to baseline methods. 

Given the fact that text-to-image generation models normally requires massive training samples and computation resources to train, an efficient fine-tuning method could benefit many researchers.

According to the experiments, the proposed methods lead to better performance on different tasks.

weaknesses.value:
Currently, the experiments are not convincing enough. For the proposed methods, one of the most important downstream applications is adapting pre-trained models to a target domain/dataset. Different from customizing with few samples, fine-tuning on downstream dataset can be easily evaluated by some commonly used metrics like FID, KID. Comparing supervised FID on a given dataset, for instance MS-COCO, of proposed methods, LoRA, full parameter fine-tuning is an important experiment.

Customize a pre-trained model with few images is an important downstream task, while it is actually very hard to evaluate the performance of different methods. Evaluating with pre-trained models (e.g. CLIP) may not be convincing enough because the novel concepts contained in new images could be outliers. It is actually hard to judge whether identity of target concept is well preserved. Thus human evaluation is suggested to be added. What's more, the method should be able to generate images of different styles (pencil drawing, oil painting), which are shown in related papers, these results are also suggested to be added in the paper.


Some experimental details are not clear enough (please see some questions below).

questions.value:
1. What is the $\theta$ in $z=cos(\theta)$ in Figure 2 of section 3.1?

2. Can the authors provide reference for the statement finetuning essentially aims to train the model while implicitly minimizing $\Vert M - M^0\Vert $?

3. Can the authors provide fine-tuning time in seconds/minutes of different methods, and comparison of sampling time with same number of steps at testing?

4. In Figure 5, there are many details lost in the given examples. How will the results be if using a much larger $\epsilon$? For this example, can the author add results of OFT and DreamBooth (which is provided in their paper Appendix) into Figure 5?

summary.value:
This work proposes Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), a new finetuning method for t2i diffusion models, centered on maintaining the hyperspherical energy from the pretrained model during finetuning to preserve semantic structures. It also introduces Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT), a variant that limits angular deviation from the pretrained model, thus preserving generative performance from pretraining.
OFT is different from LoRA, since it does not assume a low-rank structure for weight updates and instead udpates weights using layer-shared orthogonal transformations.
OFT shows good results for subject-driven and controllable generation tasks.

strengths.value:
1. From my experience, neuron angle is indeed very important and it's interesting that this paper brings this to light with rigorous arguments and some nice toy experiments.
2. The idea of OFT is solid and well-motivated. But there are questions as to the effectiveness compared to other less-well motivated alternatives such as LoRA.
3. I do think the exploration of this idea is worthwhile and this is the reason that I am still voting positively, even given my reservations on evaluation.
4. Supp. material is solid with many more examples and some good nuggets of insight (e.g. tuning conv layers is not very impactful).

weaknesses.value:
1. DB does not add additional inference overhead (L. 293)
2. Although the idea makes sense, and is an interesting way to see the problem, it is hard to know whether the empirical improvements are enough. Specifically, it seems like some metrics are better (subject fidelity, quality) and some are worse (prompt fidelity, by very little, could be negligible). But there is no user study, which could put these results in perspective. These metrics are not nearly as strong as a user study and a user study could show the real benefits of the method. This is my main reservation with regards to this work.
3. My second reservation is that, for low ranks, it would be great to have comparisons with LoRA (w/ equal number of parameters, since OFT is more parameter efficient at equal rank)

limitations.value:
Societal impact seems to be missing, although is an extension of other personalization methods such as Dreambooth etc.
Failure cases would be important for this paper - specifically, when does OFT do less well than LoRA or DB?

summary.value: This paper proposes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning algorithm that preserves the so-called "hyperspherical energy" to achieve a great trade-off between prevervation and generalization and high training efficiency. The authors conduct experiments on subject-driven generation and controllable generation, which both can improve the image generation quality as compared with other SOTA methods.

strengths.value:
1. This paper presents the orthogonal finetuning idea clearly. It provides two toy examples to help readers understand the motivation of this paper.
2. The core idea of orthogonal finetuning is straightforward and easy to understand. The authors also cite some theoretical papers about "hyperspherical energy" to support their motivation and algorithmic foundation.
3. This paper provides another perspective for the field of PEFT other than LoRA, which may excite more interesting works and discussions on this important topic.
4. The authors conduct two experiments: subject-driven generation and controllable generation based on Dreambooth and Controlnet, both of which demonstrate their effectiveness.

weaknesses.value:
1. The "subject-driven generation" introduced in related work is inadequate. Most works you mentioned are about image-editing and some recent dreambooth-like subject-driven finetuing works are not included, such as P+, DisenBooth, Cones 
  
Voynov, Andrey, et al. "$ P+ $: Extended Textual Conditioning in Text-to-Image Generation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.09522 (2023).
  
Liu, Zhiheng, et al. "Cones: Concept neurons in diffusion models for customized generation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.05125 (2023).
  
Chen, Hong, et al. "DisenBooth: Disentangled Parameter-Efficient Tuning for Subject-Driven Text-to-Image Generation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.03374 (2023).

Although this work may be close to your submission time, you'd better add some discussion or comparisons with this kind of work.

2. In Table 1 and Table 2, the statistical difference between COFT and OFT is very marginal; how can you draw the conclusion that COFT is better than OFT?

3. In the experiment section, no specific-domain finetuning comparisons between OFT and LoRA  are provided. Since LoRA is widely used in many downstream specific-domain finetuning, I'd like to see some further comparisons and discussion.

questions.value:
1. In Sec. 3.1, you say "orthogonal transformation is a sweet spot between flexibility and regularity." How can you draw the conclusion? lack some theoretical or experimental proof.
2. Figure 3 is the "controllable generation experiment using the setting of ControlNet". The results of controlnet without orthogonal finetuning (the original controlnet training ?) seem to collapse totally. Is it reasonable?
3. In line 197, I don't understand why you define HE(W) as this equation. Any reference?
4. In line 218, how to ensure that Q is a skew-symmetric matrix during code implementation? There is no explanation here or in the appendix.

title.value: Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning

abstract.value: Large text-to-image diffusion models have impressive capabilities in generating photorealistic images from text prompts. How to effectively guide or control these powerful models to perform different downstream tasks becomes an important open problem. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a principled finetuning method -- Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), for adapting text-to-image diffusion models to downstream tasks. Unlike existing methods, OFT can provably preserve hyperspherical energy which characterizes the pairwise neuron relationship on the unit hypersphere. We find that this property is crucial for preserving the semantic generation ability of text-to-image diffusion models. To improve finetuning stability, we further propose Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) which imposes an additional radius constraint to the hypersphere. Specifically, we consider two important finetuning text-to-image tasks: subject-driven generation where the goal is to generate subject-specific images given a few images of a subject and a text prompt, and controllable generation where the goal is to enable the model to take in additional control signals. We empirically show that our OFT framework outperforms existing methods in generation quality and convergence speed.

TLDR.value: A simple yet effective method for finetuning large text-to-image diffusion models

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return    

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=openreview.api.Note(
                id=submission.id
            ),
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
